entities.name: Animal Cell
entities.definition: A eukaryotic cell characteristic of animals, enclosed by a flexible plasma membrane, lacking a cell wall and chloroplasts, and containing membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, lysosomes, and a nucleus.
common_misconceptions: Animal cells have cell walls like plant cells (animal cells only have a flexible cell membrane).
Animal cells contain chloroplasts (animal cells obtain energy through heterotrophic nutrition and respiration).
learning_objectives: Identify major organelles in an animal cell (nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum).
Describe the function of the plasma membrane in regulating cell transport.
Compare structural features of animal and plant cells.
real_world_applications: Stem cell research and regenerative medicine.
Pharmacology and cellular drug toxicity testing.

entities.name: Cell
entities.definition: The basic structural, functional, and biological unit of all known living organisms. Cells carry out essential life processes, contain hereditary material, and arise from pre-existing cells.
common_misconceptions: Cells are flat two-dimensional structures as seen under standard microscope slides (cells are 3D).
All cells are identical in size and shape (cells exhibit extreme specialization and diversity).
learning_objectives: State the three principles of cell theory.
Distinguish between unicellular and multicellular organisms.
Identify major cell components common to all living cells (plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, ribosomes).
real_world_applications: Cell culture in medical diagnostics and vaccine production.

provenance.source: International Union of Biological Sciences / UNESCO Biology Framework

entities.name: Cellular Respiration
entities.definition: The metabolic process by which cells break down organic molecules (such as glucose) to release energy stored in ATP molecules, utilizing oxygen in aerobic respiration and producing carbon dioxide and water.
common_misconceptions: Cellular respiration is breathing (breathing is gas exchange at the organism level; cellular respiration is energy release at the cell level).
Plants do not undergo cellular respiration (plants continuously undergo cellular respiration to power cell work).
learning_objectives: Write the chemical equation for aerobic cellular respiration.
Distinguish aerobic respiration (with oxygen) from anaerobic respiration / fermentation (without oxygen).
Describe the role of mitochondria as the primary site of ATP generation in eukaryotic cells.
real_world_applications: Exercise physiology, metabolic rate measurement, and athletic training.
Fermentation in bread baking, brewing, and industrial biotechnology.

provenance.source: International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

entities.name: Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA)
entities.definition: A double-stranded helical nucleic acid molecule storing genetic instructions used in the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known living organisms and many viruses.
common_misconceptions: DNA is found in all body cells equally except red blood cells (mature human red blood cells lack nuclei and DNA).
Genes and DNA are separate materials (genes are specific functional segments of DNA molecules).
learning_objectives: Describe the double-helix structure of DNA composed of nucleotide units (sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous bases A, T, C, G).
Explain complementary base pairing rules (A with T, C with G).
Describe the role of DNA in genetic inheritance and protein synthesis.
real_world_applications: Forensic DNA profiling and paternity testing.
Genetic testing for hereditary medical conditions.

provenance.source: IUPAC-IUBMB Joint Commission on Biochemical Nomenclature

entities.name: Ecosystem
entities.definition: A biological community of interacting organisms (biotic factors) together with their non-living physical and chemical environment (abiotic factors), functioning as an integrated ecological system.
common_misconceptions: Ecosystems are static and unchanging when undisturbed (ecosystems experience continuous dynamic fluctuations and succession).
Decomposers are unimportant compared to predators (decomposers recycle essential chemical nutrients without which ecosystems collapse).
learning_objectives: Distinguish biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers) from abiotic components (temperature, light, water, nutrients).
Trace energy flow (one-way) and nutrient cycling (recycled) through ecosystems.
Analyze how changes in biotic or abiotic factors affect ecosystem stability.
real_world_applications: Wildlife habitat conservation and restoration ecology.
Ecosystem service evaluation (water purification, pollination, flood control).

provenance.source: International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) / UNESCO

entities.name: Enzyme
entities.definition: A biological catalyst (typically a protein) that speeds up specific biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy without being consumed in the reaction.
common_misconceptions: Enzymes are alive or die when heated (enzymes are protein molecules that denature/lose active site shape at extreme heat or pH).
Enzymes work on any reactant (enzymes demonstrate high substrate specificity via lock-and-key / induced fit active sites).
learning_objectives: Explain how enzymes lower activation energy for metabolic reactions.
Describe the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation.
Interpret substrate concentration vs. reaction rate graphs.
real_world_applications: Digestive enzyme supplements and laundry detergent formulations.

provenance.source: International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

entities.name: Gene
entities.definition: The basic physical and functional unit of heredity, composed of a specific sequence of nucleotides along a DNA molecule that codes for a specific functional polypeptide (protein) or RNA product.
common_misconceptions: Single genes strictly dictate complex traits like intelligence or behavior (most traits are polygenic and environmentally influenced).
Mutated genes are always harmful (mutations provide genetic variation essential for natural selection and evolution).
learning_objectives: Define a gene as a functional segment of DNA.
Explain how genes determine physical traits (phenotype) through protein expression.
Distinguish between dominant and recessive alleles of a gene.
real_world_applications: Gene editing technologies (CRISPR-Cas9) and gene therapy.
Agricultural crop breeding for drought and disease resistance.

entities.name: Homeostasis
entities.definition: The maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature, pH, water and solute balance, glucose levels) within living organisms despite changes in the external environment, achieved through regulatory feedback mechanisms.
common_misconceptions: Homeostasis means conditions never change (it means conditions are kept within a narrow functional range, with continuous adjustment).
Only warm-blooded animals maintain homeostasis (all living organisms regulate some internal conditions).
Homeostasis is a static set point rather than dynamic balance (it is a dynamic equilibrium maintained by negative feedback).
learning_objectives: Define homeostasis and give examples of regulated internal conditions.
Explain negative feedback using body temperature or blood glucose as examples.
Relate homeostasis to enzyme function and cell survival.
real_world_applications: Clinical monitoring of blood glucose in diabetes.

entities.name: Natural Selection
entities.definition: The evolutionary process by which organisms possessing heritable traits better suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce at higher rates, passing advantageous alleles to subsequent generations.
common_misconceptions: Natural selection involves intentional self-adaptation by individual organisms (adaptation occurs across populations over generations).
Natural selection leads to ultimate perfection in organisms (selection optimizes survival and reproduction relative to current environmental pressures).
learning_objectives: State the four conditions required for natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction, differential reproductive success.
Explain how environmental selective pressures drive evolutionary change in populations.
Describe examples of rapid natural selection (e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria, peppered moths).
real_world_applications: Managing antibiotic and pesticide resistance in medicine and agriculture.
Conservation biology and predicting species responses to climate change.

provenance.source: International Union of Biological Sciences / UNESCO Biology Framework

entities.name: Nucleus
entities.definition: The membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains most of the cell's genetic material (DNA) and directs cell activities such as growth, metabolism, and reproduction.
common_misconceptions: Every cell has a nucleus (mature red blood cells and prokaryotes lack a nucleus).
The nucleus is the same as the whole cell's control in prokaryotes (prokaryotes have no nucleus at all; their genetic material floats in the cytoplasm).
The nuclear membrane is not selective (the nuclear envelope regulates what enters and leaves the nucleus).
learning_objectives: Identify the nucleus and its parts (nuclear membrane, nucleoplasm, nucleolus, chromatin).
Describe the nucleus as the storehouse of hereditary information.
Distinguish eukaryotic cells (with nucleus) from prokaryotic cells (without).
real_world_applications: Cancer diagnosis based on abnormal nuclear morphology.

entities.name: Osmosis
entities.definition: The net movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration (higher water concentration) to a region of higher solute concentration (lower water concentration), equalizing concentration by water flow.
common_misconceptions: Osmosis moves solute particles through the membrane (osmosis moves the solvent — water — while solutes stay behind).
Osmosis and diffusion are identical (osmosis is a special case of diffusion — the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane).
Water moves toward where there is more water (water moves toward the higher solute concentration to dilute it).
learning_objectives: Define osmosis as the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
Predict the direction of water movement given solution concentrations.
Distinguish hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions and their effects on cells.
real_world_applications: Rehydration of dried fruits and pickling of vegetables.
Water uptake by plant roots and turgor in plant cells.

entities.name: Photosynthesis
entities.definition: The biological process by which autotrophic organisms (such as plants and algae) convert light energy into stored chemical energy in glucose, using carbon dioxide and water while releasing oxygen as a byproduct.
common_misconceptions: Photosynthesis occurs to produce energy for plants instead of storing energy as carbohydrates.
Photosynthesis occurs during the day while cellular respiration only occurs at night (respiration occurs continuously).
Plants obtain their primary mass from soil nutrients rather than carbon dioxide gas from air.
learning_objectives: State the balanced chemical equation for oxygenic photosynthesis.
Describe the role of chlorophyll in absorbing light energy.
Explain how photosynthesis drives carbon cycling and energy flow in ecosystems.
real_world_applications: Atmospheric oxygen regulation and carbon sequestration.

entities.name: Plant Cell
entities.definition: A eukaryotic cell characteristic of plants, distinguished by a rigid cellulose cell wall, a large central vacuole for turgor pressure, and plastids such as chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
common_misconceptions: Plant cells do not perform cellular respiration (plant cells perform both photosynthesis and respiration).
Plant cells lack cell membranes (plant cells have a cell membrane inside the rigid cell wall).
learning_objectives: Identify key structures unique to plant cells (cell wall, chloroplasts, central vacuole).
Explain the role of the cell wall and vacuole in providing mechanical support.
Compare plant cell structures with animal cells.
real_world_applications: Biofuel development and plant tissue culture.

entities.name: Acid
entities.definition: A chemical substance that releases hydrogen ions (H⁺ or hydronium H₃O⁺) in aqueous solution, tastes sour, turns blue litmus paper red, has a pH less than 7, and reacts with bases to form salts and water.
common_misconceptions: All acids burn skin and dissolve everything (many weak acids are safe and essential in biological systems, e.g. citric acid, amino acids).
Strong acids and concentrated acids mean the same thing (strength is degree of ionization; concentration is amount of acid per volume).
learning_objectives: Define an acid according to Arrhenius (H⁺ producer) and Brønsted-Lowry (proton donor) models.
Distinguish strong acids (fully ionized) from weak acids (partially ionized).
Describe characteristic acid reactions with metals, carbonates, and bases.
real_world_applications: Lead-acid car batteries (sulfuric acid) and food preservation (vinegar/acetic acid).

entities.name: Atom
entities.definition: The smallest unit of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element. An atom consists of a dense central nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by a cloud of electrons.
common_misconceptions: Atoms are solid spheres with fixed orbits like solar systems (electrons exist in probability clouds).
Atoms can be seen with optical microscopes (atoms are smaller than wavelengths of visible light).
learning_objectives: Describe the internal structure of an atom (protons, neutrons, electrons).
Explain how the number of protons defines an element's atomic number.
Relate atomic structure to chemical reactivity.

entities.name: Base
entities.definition: A chemical substance that reacts with acids to form salt and water, accepts protons (H⁺), or releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in aqueous solution (alkali). Bases taste bitter, feel slippery, turn red litmus paper blue, and have a pH greater than 7.
common_misconceptions: Bases are completely harmless compared to acids (strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide cause severe chemical burns).
All bases are soluble in water (alkalis are water-soluble bases; insoluble bases like copper oxide are not alkalis).
learning_objectives: Define a base (proton acceptor / hydroxide producer) and distinguish alkalis from insoluble bases.
Explain strong vs. weak bases in terms of dissociation.
Describe neutralization reactions of bases with acids.
real_world_applications: Household cleaning products (ammonia, drain cleaner / sodium hydroxide).

entities.name: Balanced Chemical Equation
entities.definition: A symbolic representation of a chemical reaction showing reactants on the left and products on the right, with coefficient ratios balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is conserved across the arrow.
common_misconceptions: Coefficients and subscripts can be changed freely to balance an equation (coefficients may change; subscripts define the substance and must not).
Balancing changes the identity of the substances (balancing only adjusts amounts, never the compounds involved).
The arrow means equality of amounts (it indicates transformation; total atom count is conserved, not the number of molecules).
learning_objectives: Write and balance chemical equations for common reactions.
Interpret a balanced equation in terms of particles, moles, and mass.
Verify that atoms of each element are conserved.
real_world_applications: Stoichiometric calculation of reactants and products in industry.
Fuel combustion tuning and air quality modeling.

entities.name: Chemical Reaction
entities.definition: A process in which one or more substances (reactants) are chemically transformed into one or more different substances (products) through the breaking and forming of chemical bonds, conserving total mass and atoms.
common_misconceptions: Atoms are destroyed or created during chemical reactions (atoms are only rearranged).
Mass changes significantly during chemical reactions in closed systems (mass is conserved).
learning_objectives: Identify evidence of chemical reactions (color change, gas evolution, precipitate, temperature change).
Write and balance chemical equations demonstrating mass conservation.
Distinguish between reactants and products.
real_world_applications: Combustion in engines and power plants.

entities.name: Combustion
entities.definition: A rapid chemical reaction between a substance and an oxidant (usually oxygen) that releases heat and light. Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and soot.
common_misconceptions: Combustion can occur without oxygen (combustion requires an oxidant, normally oxygen in air).
Fire and combustion are the same thing (fire is the visible, observable event of combustion, not the reaction itself).
Complete combustion is always achieved with plenty of fuel (complete combustion needs sufficient oxygen, not more fuel).
learning_objectives: Describe combustion as an exothermic oxidation reaction.
Distinguish complete from incomplete combustion and their products.
Relate combustion to everyday fuels and their environmental effects.
real_world_applications: Burning fossil fuels for energy and transport.
Cooking and heating with gas burners.

entities.name: Chemical Compound
entities.definition: A pure substance formed when two or more different chemical elements are chemically bonded together in a fixed stoichiometric ratio. Compounds have chemical properties distinct from their constituent elements.
common_misconceptions: Compounds retain the physical and chemical properties of their constituent elements (e.g., sodium and chlorine vs. table salt).
Mixtures and compounds are identical (mixtures are physically combined without fixed ratios or chemical bonds).
learning_objectives: Define a chemical compound and distinguish it from a mixture.
Interpret chemical formulae representing molecular and ionic compounds.
Explain how chemical bonding creates compounds with unique properties.

entities.name: Covalent Bond
entities.definition: A chemical bond formed when two non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons, achieving stable noble-gas electron configurations through mutual electrostatic attraction between shared electrons and nuclei.
common_misconceptions: Covalent bonding involves transfer of electrons (covalent bonding involves sharing of electron pairs).
All covalent compounds are simple small molecules (some form giant covalent network structures like diamond and quartz).
learning_objectives: Draw Lewis dot structures for single, double, and triple covalent bonds (e.g. H₂, O₂, N₂).
Distinguish simple molecular covalent structures from giant covalent networks.
Relate covalent molecular structures to low melting/boiling points.
real_world_applications: Organic chemistry, polymers, and plastics manufacturing.

entities.name: Diffusion
entities.definition: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, driven by the random thermal motion of particles, until concentrations equalize.
common_misconceptions: Diffusion happens only in gases (diffusion occurs in gases, liquids, and across solutions).
Particles move because they are pushed toward empty space (particles move randomly; net flow arises from statistical imbalance, not repulsion).
Higher temperature slows diffusion (higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy and speeds diffusion).
learning_objectives: Explain diffusion in terms of random particle motion.
Describe factors that affect the rate of diffusion (temperature, particle size, concentration gradient).
Distinguish diffusion from osmosis.
real_world_applications: Spreading of perfume or cooking smells through a room.
Gas exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in lungs.

entities.name: Electron
entities.definition: A stable subatomic particle carrying a negative elementary electric charge (-1e) and a mass approximately 1/1836th of a proton (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg), occupying atomic orbitals surrounding the nucleus.
common_misconceptions: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed circular paths like planets (electrons exist in 3D atomic orbitals/probability clouds).
Electrons move at the speed of light in wires (electron drift speed is slow, but electromagnetic signal propagates fast).
learning_objectives: State the charge, mass, and location of electrons in an atom.
Explain how valence electrons determine chemical bonding and reactivity.
Relate electron arrangement to periodic table group properties.
real_world_applications: Electron microscopy and cathode ray tubes.

entities.name: Chemical Element
entities.definition: A pure chemical substance consisting of atoms that all have the same number of protons in their atomic nuclei. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.
common_misconceptions: Elements and compounds are the same thing (compounds contain two or more different elements).
Molecules can only be compounds (some elements exist naturally as diatomic or polyatomic molecules, e.g., O₂, N₂).
learning_objectives: Define a chemical element in terms of atomic number.
Locate and identify elements on the periodic table.
Distinguish between elemental substances and chemical compounds.

entities.name: Ionic Bond
entities.definition: A chemical bond formed through the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, resulting from the complete transfer of one or more valence electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
common_misconceptions: Ionic compounds consist of individual discrete molecules (ionic compounds form continuous 3D giant crystal lattices).
Ionic bonds exist in liquid solution without ion dissociation (in water, ionic lattices dissociate into solvated free ions).
learning_objectives: Describe electron transfer leading to cation and anion formation.
Explain how electrostatic forces hold ionic crystal lattices together.
Predict formula units for binary ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl, MgO).
real_world_applications: Electrolyte solutions in batteries and physiological fluids.

entities.name: Matter
entities.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space by occupying volume. Matter is composed of fundamental particles and exists in various physical states depending on thermal energy and pressure.
common_misconceptions: Energy and matter are the same thing at introductory levels (energy has no mass or volume).
Gases do not count as matter because they are invisible (gases have mass and occupy volume).
learning_objectives: Define matter in terms of mass and volume.
Distinguish between physical and chemical properties of matter.
Classify samples of matter as pure substances or mixtures.
real_world_applications: Environmental monitoring of air and water quality.

provenance.source: IUPAC Gold Book / UNESCO Science Education Framework

entities.name: Mixture
entities.definition: A physical combination of two or more substances that are not chemically bonded, can vary in composition, and can be separated by physical means. Homogeneous mixtures are uniform throughout; heterogeneous mixtures are not.
common_misconceptions: A mixture and a compound are the same (mixtures keep the properties of their components and separate physically; compounds form new substances with new properties).
Every mixture looks uniform (only homogeneous mixtures do; heterogeneous mixtures, like sand in water, are visibly uneven).
Separating a mixture changes its nature (physical separation preserves the identity of the components).
learning_objectives: Distinguish a mixture from a pure substance and from a compound.
Classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Describe physical separation methods (filtration, distillation, evaporation, chromatography).
real_world_applications: Separation of crude oil by fractional distillation.
Air and seawater as naturally occurring mixtures.

entities.name: Neutralization Reaction
entities.definition: A chemical reaction between an acid and a base (or alkali) producing a salt and water, in which hydrogen ions (H⁺) from the acid react with hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from the base to form neutral water molecules (H₂O).
common_misconceptions: Neutralization always results in a solution of exactly pH 7 (neutralization of weak acids or bases can produce acidic or basic salt solutions).
Neutralization destroys energy (neutralization is exothermic and releases heat).
learning_objectives: Write word and balanced chemical equations for acid-base neutralization.
Predict the specific salt formed from given acids and bases (e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O).
Explain how neutralization changes solution pH toward neutral.
real_world_applications: Agricultural liming to neutralize acidic soil.
Treatment of industrial acidic wastewater prior to discharge.

entities.name: Periodic Table of Elements
entities.definition: A tabular arrangement of chemical elements ordered by increasing atomic number, displaying recurring (periodic) trends in chemical and physical properties across periods (rows) and groups (columns).
common_misconceptions: Elements in the periodic table are ordered by atomic mass (they are strictly ordered by atomic number Z).
All elements in a group have identical physical states (groups share chemical reactivity patterns, but physical states vary).
learning_objectives: Locate elements by period number and group number on the periodic table.
Explain why elements in the same group exhibit similar chemical properties.
Identify major categories: alkali metals, alkaline earths, transition metals, halogens, noble gases.
real_world_applications: Predicting chemical reactivity and bond formation in chemistry labs.
Discovering new materials and semiconductor doping.

provenance.source: IUPAC Periodic Table of the Elements

entities.name: pH Scale
entities.definition: A logarithmic scale measuring the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution, defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration (pH = -log₁₀[H⁺]), ranging from 0 (highly acidic) to 14 (highly alkaline), with 7 being neutral.
common_misconceptions: A change of 1 pH unit represents a 1-fold change in acidity (pH is logarithmic: a 1-unit change is a 10-fold change in H⁺ concentration).
Neutral pH is always 7 regardless of temperature (neutral pH equals 7 at 25 °C, but changes slightly with temperature).
learning_objectives: Interpret values on the 0–14 pH scale (acidic < 7, neutral = 7, basic > 7).
Use indicators (litmus, universal indicator, pH meters) to estimate solution pH.
Calculate H⁺ concentration from pH and vice versa.
real_world_applications: Soil testing for agricultural crop suitability.
Swimming pool and aquarium water quality maintenance.

provenance.source: IUPAC Quantities, Units and Symbols in Physical Chemistry

entities.name: Proton
entities.definition: A stable subatomic particle occurring in all atomic nuclei, carrying a positive elementary electric charge (+1e) and a mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit (1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
common_misconceptions: Protons leave the nucleus during ordinary chemical reactions (only outer electrons are transferred or shared).
Changing the number of protons does not change the element (proton count strictly determines elemental identity).
learning_objectives: Identify the charge, mass, and location of protons in an atom.
Relate proton count (atomic number Z) to elemental identity on the periodic table.
Calculate net atomic/ionic charge from proton and electron numbers.
real_world_applications: Proton beam radiation therapy in cancer treatment.
Mass spectrometry for chemical structural analysis.

entities.name: Salt
entities.definition: An ionic compound formed when the hydrogen ion of an acid is replaced by a metal ion (or ammonium ion), typically produced by neutralization of an acid with a base. Common table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
common_misconceptions: Salt means only sodium chloride (a salt is any ionic compound formed from acid-base chemistry; NaCl is one example).
All salts are safe to eat (many salts such as ammonium nitrate or heavy-metal salts are toxic or hazardous).
Salts are always neutral (salts of weak acids or weak bases can form acidic or basic solutions).
learning_objectives: Define a salt and describe how it forms from an acid and a base.
Give examples of common salts and their uses.
Predict the salt produced by a given acid-base pair.
real_world_applications: De-icing roads (sodium chloride lowers the freezing point).

entities.name: Earth Atmosphere
entities.definition: The layer of gases surrounding Earth, retained by Earth's gravity, composed primarily of nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%), which absorbs ultraviolet radiation, warms the surface via the greenhouse effect, and regulates weather.
common_misconceptions: Space begins abruptly where the atmosphere stops (atmospheric density decreases continuously with altitude).
The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful (the natural greenhouse effect makes Earth habitable).
learning_objectives: Describe the gas composition and vertical structure of the atmosphere (troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere).
Explain how atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.
Analyze the natural greenhouse effect and thermal radiation absorption.
real_world_applications: Aviation and satellite orbit decay management.
Climate change mitigation and air quality control.

entities.name: Big Bang Theory
entities.definition: The prevailing cosmological model describing the early development and metric expansion of the universe from an extremely hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
common_misconceptions: The Big Bang was an explosion into pre-existing space (the Big Bang describes the expansion of space itself everywhere).
The universe expands into empty outer space (space itself is expanding between distant galaxy clusters).
learning_objectives: Summarize key observational evidence supporting the Big Bang: cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) and galactic redshift (Hubble's law).
Describe the age and continuous metric expansion of the observable universe.
Distinguish scientific cosmological consensus from speculative hypotheses.
real_world_applications: Radio astronomy telescope development and satellite microwave detectors.
Fundamental physics research into elemental nucleosynthesis.

provenance.source: International Astronomical Union (IAU) / NASA Cosmology Framework

entities.name: Earth System
entities.definition: The integrated complex of physical, chemical, biological, and geological processes interacting across Earth's four major interconnected spheres: the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere.
common_misconceptions: Earth's spheres operate independently of one another (they are constantly exchanging matter and energy).
Human activity is external to the Earth system (human activities are an integral component of biosphere interactions).
learning_objectives: Identify and describe the four primary Earth spheres.
Explain examples of energy and matter transport between spheres (e.g. water and carbon cycles).
Analyze human impacts on Earth system feedback mechanisms.
real_world_applications: Global climate modeling and weather forecasting.
Natural resource management and environmental policy.

provenance.source: NASA Earth System Science Framework / AGU

entities.name: Greenhouse Effect
entities.definition: The process by which greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere (such as water vapor, CO₂, CH₄) absorb outgoing infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-radiate thermal energy in all directions, warming the lower atmosphere.
common_misconceptions: The greenhouse effect functions like a physical glass greenhouse preventing convection (the atmospheric effect operates primarily by absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation).
The natural greenhouse effect is harmful (without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be approximately -18 °C).
learning_objectives: Explain energy balance between incoming solar radiation (shortwave) and outgoing terrestrial radiation (longwave/infrared).
Identify major greenhouse gases and their relative warming potentials.
Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activities.
real_world_applications: Global climate modeling and carbon footprint accounting.
Renewable energy policy and emission reduction technologies.

entities.name: Plate Tectonics
entities.definition: The unifying geological theory explaining that Earth's rigid outer shell (lithosphere) is divided into several large plates that move slowly over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection currents.
common_misconceptions: Continents float on liquid ocean magma (tectonic plates consist of rigid lithospheric rock moving over ductile asthenosphere).
Tectonic plate movement is fast and noticeable daily (plates move at rates of 1–10 cm per year).
learning_objectives: Describe the three types of plate boundaries: convergent, divergent, and transform.
Relate plate tectonics to earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building, and oceanic trench formation.
Explain mantle convection as the primary thermal driving mechanism for plate motion.
real_world_applications: Earthquake hazard assessment and building code engineering.
Geothermal energy site exploration and mineral resource discovery.

provenance.source: USGS / AGU Earth Science Education Framework

entities.name: Rock Cycle
entities.definition: The continuous transformation of the three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — through weathering, erosion, deposition, burial, heat, pressure, and melting, driven by Earth's internal heat and surface processes.
common_misconceptions: Rocks are permanent and unchanging (rocks continuously transform between the three families over geological time).
The rock cycle moves only in one direction (rocks can take many different pathways through the cycle).
Magma is found only inside volcanoes (magma is melt within the crust and upper mantle; lava is melt at the surface).
learning_objectives: Describe the three rock families and how each forms.
Trace pathways through the rock cycle.
Relate the rock cycle to plate tectonics and Earth's internal heat.
real_world_applications: Geological resource exploration (minerals, fossil fuels, groundwater).
Understanding volcanic hazard and earthquake risk.
Interpreting Earth's history from rock records.

provenance.source: NASA Earth System Science Framework / AGU

entities.name: Cause of Astronomical Seasons
entities.definition: The cyclical variation in temperature and daylight duration across Earth's year, caused primarily by Earth's 23.5° axial tilt relative to its orbital plane around the Sun, changing solar incidence angle and daylight length.
common_misconceptions: Seasons are caused by Earth being significantly closer to the Sun in summer (Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January during Northern Hemisphere winter).
Both Northern and Southern hemispheres experience summer at the same time (hemispheres experience opposite seasons due to axial tilt orientation).
learning_objectives: Explain how Earth's 23.5° axial tilt alters solar angle of incidence and daylight duration throughout the year.
Interpret solstices and equinoxes on orbital diagrams.
Disprove the distance misconception using orbital data (perihelion vs. aphelion distance differences).
real_world_applications: Agricultural crop planting schedules and solar energy system tilt design.
Climate zone classification and architectural daylighting.

provenance.source: NASA Science Framework / IAU Astronomy Education

entities.name: Solar System
entities.definition: The gravitationally bound system consisting of the Sun, eight planets and their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and interplanetary material, orbiting the Sun.
common_misconceptions: The planets orbit the Sun because the Sun is the biggest object (planets orbit because of the mutual gravitational attraction, dominated by the Sun's mass).
Pluto is counted among the eight major planets (Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet).
All solar system bodies orbit in the same plane and direction because of imposed rules (they formed from a single rotating protoplanetary disk).
learning_objectives: Describe the structure and members of the solar system.
Explain the role of gravity in holding the solar system together.
Relate Earth's motion (orbit and axial tilt) to seasons.
real_world_applications: Understanding Earth's place and habitability in the solar system.

entities.name: Water Cycle
entities.definition: The continuous circulation of water between the atmosphere, Earth's surface, and underground reservoirs through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, and runoff, driven by solar energy and gravity.
common_misconceptions: The water cycle creates new water (the total water on Earth is essentially constant; the cycle only moves and changes its state).
Evaporation and boiling are the same (evaporation occurs at any temperature at the surface; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at the boiling point).
Rainwater is completely pure (rain picks up dissolved gases and particles as it falls).
learning_objectives: Trace the movement of water through the stages of the water cycle.
Identify the energy sources that drive the water cycle (solar energy, gravity).
Explain the role of the atmosphere and oceans as water reservoirs.
real_world_applications: Freshwater resource management and irrigation scheduling.
Understanding droughts, floods, and groundwater recharge.

entities.name: Engineering Design Process
entities.definition: An iterative problem-solving methodology involving problem definition, criteria and constraint identification, concept generation, modeling, prototyping, testing, trade-off evaluation, and design optimization.
common_misconceptions: Engineering design is a linear step-by-step procedure (it is iterative with multiple feedback loops).
Engineering design is the same as scientific inquiry (science seeks to explain natural phenomena; engineering solves practical human problems under constraints).
learning_objectives: Describe the iterative steps of the engineering design process.
Distinguish design criteria (requirements) from design constraints (limitations).
Evaluate trade-offs between competing design criteria (e.g. cost vs safety vs performance).
real_world_applications: Biomedical device development and software engineering.

entities.name: Observation vs. Inference
entities.definition: The epistemic distinction between direct empirical data gathered through sensing/measurement (observation) and the logical explanation or conclusion derived from those data based on prior knowledge (inference).
common_misconceptions: Inferences are facts (inferences are interpretations that require logical justification and testing).
Scientific theories are just guesses (scientific theories are well-supported explanatory frameworks based on extensive observations).
learning_objectives: Distinguish direct observations from logical inferences in scientific reports.
Explain how multiple inferences can be constructed from the same set of observations.
Evaluate the strength of evidence supporting a scientific inference.
real_world_applications: Diagnostic medical reasoning and scientific peer review.

provenance.source: OECD PISA Epistemic Knowledge Framework / NSTA Nature of Science

entities.name: Acceleration
entities.definition: The rate of change of velocity with respect to time; a vector quantity. Acceleration occurs whenever an object's velocity changes — whether in magnitude, direction, or both.
common_misconceptions: Velocity and acceleration always point in the same direction (acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity).
Acceleration always means speeding up (slowing down and changing direction are also acceleration).
If velocity is zero, acceleration must be zero (an object can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration, e.g., at the top of a vertical throw).
If speed is constant, acceleration must be zero (changing direction at constant speed is still acceleration).
learning_objectives: Define acceleration as a vector quantity.
Calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
Distinguish between positive, negative, and zero acceleration.
Interpret acceleration from velocity-time graphs.
Explain situations where velocity and acceleration have different directions.
key_experiments: Rolling a ball down an inclined plane and measuring its increasing speed.
Motion sensor experiments recording velocity vs. time during acceleration.

entities.name: Amplitude
entities.definition: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position. Amplitude determines the energy carried by the wave — greater amplitude means greater energy.
common_misconceptions: Amplitude is the wavelength (amplitude is height; wavelength is distance between cycles).
Amplitude affects wave speed (wave speed depends on the medium, not amplitude).
learning_objectives: Define amplitude and identify it on a wave diagram.
Relate amplitude to wave energy.
Compare amplitudes of different waves.

entities.name: Atomic Structure
entities.definition: The structure of an atom as a dense, positively charged nucleus (containing protons and neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons in orbitals. The number of protons determines the element.
common_misconceptions: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed paths like planets (electrons exist in probability clouds/orbitals).
The atom is mostly solid matter (the atom is mostly empty space).
All atoms of an element have the same number of neutrons (isotopes vary in neutron count).
learning_objectives: Describe the atom as a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
Distinguish between protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Define atomic number and mass number.
Explain isotopes.

entities.name: Buoyancy
entities.definition: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object immersed in it. This force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object (Archimedes' principle).
common_misconceptions: Floating objects experience no buoyant force (they do — it equals their weight).
Only light objects float (shape matters — steel ships float).
Buoyancy depends on the object's mass (it depends on the fluid's density and displaced volume).
learning_objectives: Explain buoyancy as an upward force from a fluid.
State Archimedes' principle.
Calculate buoyant force.
Explain why objects float or sink.
key_experiments: Measuring buoyant force on an object in water.
Verifying Archimedes' principle.

entities.name: Change of State
entities.definition: The transition of matter between solid, liquid, and gas phases. During a change of state, temperature remains constant as energy is used to break or form intermolecular bonds.
common_misconceptions: Temperature rises during melting/boiling (it stays constant until the change is complete).
Boiling only happens at 100°C (boiling point depends on pressure).
Steam at 100°C is not dangerous (it contains large amounts of latent heat).
learning_objectives: Describe melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation, and deposition.
Explain why temperature is constant during a change of state.
Calculate energy required for changes of state using Q = mL.
Interpret heating curves.
key_experiments: Heating ice to water to steam and recording temperature over time.

entities.name: Law of Conservation of Energy
entities.definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one object to another or converted from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
entities.equation: E_initial = E_final ; KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f (conservative systems)
common_misconceptions: Energy can be "used up" (energy is conserved; it only changes form).
Perpetual motion machines are possible (they violate conservation of energy).
Friction creates energy (friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy).
Conservation of energy applies only to mechanical energy (it applies to all forms).
learning_objectives: State the law of conservation of energy.
Apply conservation of energy to solve problems involving energy transfers.
Analyze situations where mechanical energy is conserved vs. not conserved.
Explain why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

entities.name: Coulomb's Law
entities.definition: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
common_misconceptions: Coulomb's law applies to charges of any size (it is exact for point charges).
Force between charges depends on the medium (it does — the constant k changes).
Coulomb's law is the same as Newton's gravitation (both are inverse-square but differ in detail).
learning_objectives: State Coulomb's law.
Calculate electrostatic force between two charges.
Compare electrostatic and gravitational forces.
Explain the inverse-square nature of electrostatic force.

entities.name: Electric Current
entities.definition: The flow of electric charge through a conductor. Current is measured as the rate of flow of charge past a point in a circuit.
common_misconceptions: Current is "used up" by components (current is the same throughout a series circuit).
Current flows from negative to positive (conventional current flows from positive to negative).
Higher voltage always means more current (depends on resistance too).
learning_objectives: Define current as the rate of flow of charge.
Calculate current from charge and time.
Measure current using an ammeter.
Distinguish between conventional current and electron flow.

entities.name: Density
entities.definition: The mass per unit volume of a substance. Density determines whether objects float or sink in fluids.
common_misconceptions: Heavy objects always sink (it depends on density, not just mass).
Density is the same as weight (density is mass/volume; weight is a force).
All solids are denser than all liquids (ice floats on water — ice is less dense).
learning_objectives: Define density as mass per unit volume.
Calculate density from mass and volume.
Explain floating and sinking in terms of density.
Measure density of regular and irregular objects.
real_world_applications: Ship design (steel ships float because they displace enough water).
Hot air balloons (less dense air rises).
key_experiments: Measuring density of a regular solid and an irregular solid using displacement.

entities.name: Displacement
entities.definition: The change in position of an object, measured as a straight-line vector from the initial position to the final position. Displacement has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity.
common_misconceptions: Displacement is always equal to distance (they differ when the path curves or reverses).
Displacement depends on the path taken (displacement depends only on start and end points).
learning_objectives: Define displacement as a vector quantity.
Calculate displacement from position data.
Distinguish displacement from distance in multi-segment motion.

entities.name: Distance
entities.definition: The total length of the path traveled between two positions, regardless of direction. Distance is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction.
common_misconceptions: Distance and displacement are always the same (they differ whenever the path is not a straight line).
Distance can be negative (distance is always non-negative).
learning_objectives: Define distance as a scalar quantity.
Distinguish between distance and displacement.
Calculate total distance traveled from a path description.

entities.name: Efficiency
entities.definition: The ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, expressed as a percentage. No real machine can be 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated (usually as heat).
common_misconceptions: Efficiency can exceed 100% (this would violate conservation of energy).
Inefficient machines destroy energy (energy is conserved; it just becomes less useful).
All energy losses can be eliminated (second law of thermodynamics prevents this).
learning_objectives: Define efficiency as the ratio of useful output to total input.
Calculate efficiency in energy conversion processes.
Explain why efficiency is always less than 100%.
Suggest ways to improve efficiency in real systems.

entities.name: Electric Charge
entities.definition: A fundamental property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field. Charge can be positive or negative; like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
common_misconceptions: Charge is created by friction (charge is transferred, not created).
A charged object always attracts uncharged objects (a charged object can attract a neutral one through polarization).
Electrons are the only charge carriers (ions can also carry charge).
learning_objectives: Describe electric charge as a fundamental property.
Explain charging by friction, conduction, and induction.
State Coulomb's law and calculate electrostatic force.
Distinguish between conductors and insulators.
key_experiments: Charging a rod by friction and attracting small pieces of paper.

entities.name: Electric Motor
entities.definition: An electrical machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy through the interaction between a magnetic field and winding currents producing rotational force (torque).
common_misconceptions: Motors create energy out of nothing (motors convert electrical energy to mechanical energy with some heat loss).
Motors operate on electrostatic repulsion (motors operate via magnetic forces on current-carrying conductors).
learning_objectives: Explain the motor effect (force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field).
Describe the roles of the armature, commutator, field magnets, and brushes in a DC motor.
Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to predict direction of motor rotation.
real_world_applications: Electric vehicles, trains, and elevator propulsion systems.

provenance.source: IEEE / UNESCO Engineering & Physics Education Framework

entities.name: Electromagnetic Induction
entities.definition: The production of an electromotive force (voltage) across a conductor when it is exposed to a changing magnetic field. This is the principle behind electric generators.
common_misconceptions: A stationary magnet near a coil produces current (the magnetic field must be changing).
Induced voltage depends on the magnet's strength alone (it depends on the rate of change of flux).
learning_objectives: Explain electromagnetic induction.
Describe Faraday's law of induction.
Explain how generators produce electricity.
Apply Lenz's law to determine the direction of induced current.

entities.name: Electromagnetic Spectrum
entities.definition: The range of all types of electromagnetic radiation, ordered by wavelength or frequency. From longest wavelength to shortest: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
entities.equation: c = f·λ (applies to all EM waves)
common_misconceptions: All EM waves are the same (they differ in wavelength, frequency, and energy).
EM waves need a medium (they travel through vacuum).
Visible light is the only useful part of the spectrum (all parts have applications).
learning_objectives: Describe the EM spectrum in order of wavelength/frequency.
State that all EM waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
Identify uses and hazards of different parts of the spectrum.
Relate energy to frequency (higher frequency = higher energy).

entities.name: Electromagnetism
entities.definition: The branch of physics dealing with the relationship between electricity and magnetism. A changing electric field produces a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.
common_misconceptions: Electricity and magnetism are separate phenomena (they are two aspects of the same force).
Only magnets produce magnetic fields (current-carrying wires also produce them).
learning_objectives: Explain that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field.
Describe the magnetic effect of current (Oersted's experiment).
Explain the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Describe applications: electric motor, loudspeaker.
key_experiments: Oersted's experiment (compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire).

entities.name: Energy
entities.definition: The capacity to do work or produce change. Energy exists in many forms and can be transferred between objects or converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed.
common_misconceptions: Energy is a substance (energy is a property of systems, not a material).
Energy can be "used up" (energy is conserved; it only changes form).
Only moving objects have energy (stored energy — potential — exists without motion).
Heat and temperature are the same as energy (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
learning_objectives: Define energy as the capacity to do work.
Identify different forms of energy (kinetic, potential, thermal, electrical, etc.).
Explain energy transfers and conversions.
Apply the law of conservation of energy.
real_world_applications: Power generation (converting one form of energy to electrical).

entities.name: Energy Loss
entities.definition: The conversion of useful energy into forms that are not available for doing the intended work, typically thermal energy due to friction, air resistance, or other dissipative processes. Energy is conserved overall, but its usefulness decreases.
common_misconceptions: Energy is destroyed when it is "lost" (energy is conserved; it only becomes less useful).
Energy loss violates conservation of energy (it does not — total energy is conserved).
Friction creates energy (friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy).
learning_objectives: Explain what is meant by energy loss in physical systems.
Distinguish between energy conservation and energy dissipation.
Identify sources of energy loss in mechanical systems.
Calculate efficiency of energy conversion.

entities.name: Energy Sources
entities.definition: The origins of energy used by human civilization. Energy sources are classified as renewable (naturally replenished) or non-renewable (finite and depleting).
common_misconceptions: Energy can be created (energy is only converted from one form to another).
Renewable energy has no environmental impact (all energy sources have some impact).
Fossil fuels are unlimited (they are finite and depleting).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
Describe how common energy sources work.
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of different energy sources.
Explain the importance of energy conservation.
real_world_applications: Power generation (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, solar, wind).

entities.name: Equations of Motion
entities.definition: The set of kinematic equations relating displacement, initial velocity, uniform acceleration, and time for motion in a straight line under constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, and s = ½(u + v)t. They apply only when acceleration is constant.
entities.equation: v = u + at;  s = ut + ½at²;  v² = u² + 2as;  s = ½(u+v)t
common_misconceptions: Equations of motion apply whenever an object moves (they are valid only for uniform, constant acceleration).
u and v are interchangeable (u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity; swapping them changes the answer).
The equations work for any motion including circular motion (they describe straight-line kinematics only).
learning_objectives: State the four equations of motion for uniform acceleration.
Select the correct equation given the known and unknown quantities.
Solve numerical problems for displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.
real_world_applications: Calculating vehicle stopping distances and reaction distance.
Predicting the time and height of a ball thrown vertically upward.
Analyzing free fall near Earth's surface.

provenance.source: Nepal CDC SEE / CBSE / UK KS4 kinematics objectives

entities.name: Force
entities.definition: An influence that can change the motion of a body — that is, accelerate it. In classical mechanics the net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum. Force is a vector quantity.
common_misconceptions: A constant net force produces constant speed (it produces constant acceleration).
Force is a property of an object (force acts between objects; it is not possessed by one).
Objects at rest have no forces acting on them (forces can balance to give zero net force).
Heavier objects require more force to move because they have more "inertia" (inertia is resistance to acceleration, not weight).
learning_objectives: Define force as a vector quantity that causes acceleration.
Distinguish between contact and non-contact forces.
Draw free-body diagrams showing forces acting on an object.
Calculate net force from multiple forces acting on an object.
Apply F = m·a to calculate force, mass, or acceleration.
key_experiments: Measuring force using a spring balance.
Investigating the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration using a trolley and ticker-timer.

entities.name: Free Fall
entities.definition: Motion under the influence of gravitational force alone, with no other forces (especially air resistance) acting. In free fall, all objects experience the same acceleration regardless of mass, provided air resistance is negligible.
common_misconceptions: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones (in vacuum, all fall at the same rate).
Free fall means the object is falling downward (moving upward under gravity alone is also free fall).
Gravity is stronger on heavier objects (gravitational acceleration is independent of mass).
learning_objectives: Describe free fall as motion with constant acceleration due to gravity.
Use the equations of motion for free-fall calculations.
Explain why mass does not affect free-fall acceleration in vacuum.
Analyze vertical motion including both upward and downward segments.
real_world_applications: Dropping objects to measure gravitational acceleration.
key_experiments: Dropping objects of different masses in a vacuum chamber.
Measuring g using a falling object and timer.

entities.name: Frequency
entities.definition: The number of complete wave cycles passing a given point per unit time. Frequency determines the pitch of sound and the color of light.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency means larger waves (higher frequency means shorter wavelength).
Frequency depends on the medium (frequency is determined by the source; wavelength changes with medium).
learning_objectives: Define frequency and its unit (hertz).
Calculate frequency from period and vice versa.
Relate frequency to wave speed and wavelength.

entities.name: Friction
entities.definition: A contact force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of relative motion) between two surfaces in contact. Friction acts parallel to the contact surface and opposite to the direction of motion or attempted motion.
entities.equation: f = μ·N (for sliding friction; μ = coefficient of friction, N = normal force)
common_misconceptions: Friction always opposes motion (it opposes relative motion — it can also cause motion, e.g., walking).
Friction depends on contact area (for sliding friction, it depends primarily on normal force and materials).
Friction is always undesirable (without friction, we couldn't walk, drive, or hold objects).
Smooth surfaces have no friction (all surfaces have some friction; even "smooth" surfaces have microscopic irregularities).
learning_objectives: Identify the direction of frictional force in physical situations.
Distinguish between static and kinetic friction.
Explain factors affecting friction.
Analyze forces on objects with friction present.
Solve problems involving friction on horizontal and inclined surfaces.
real_world_applications: Wear on machinery (friction as a source of energy loss).
key_experiments: Measuring the force needed to start sliding an object (static friction) vs. keep it sliding (kinetic friction).
Investigating how surface type and normal force affect friction.

entities.name: Electric Generator
entities.definition: A machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction, forcing electric charge to flow through an external circuit by rotating a coil in a magnetic field.
common_misconceptions: Generators create electric charge (generators move existing free charges in conductors via magnetic induction).
Generators produce 100% efficient electrical power (some mechanical energy is dissipated as thermal energy).
learning_objectives: Explain how mechanical rotation induces an alternating electromotive force (AC voltage).
Compare alternating current (AC) generators (slip rings) with direct current (DC) generators (split-ring commutator).
Apply Fleming's right-hand rule to predict direction of induced current.
real_world_applications: Hydroelectric, wind turbine, and thermal power plant generators.
Portable emergency power generators and bicycle dynamos.

entities.name: Graphical Analysis of Motion
entities.definition: The use of graphs to represent and analyze motion. Distance-time and velocity-time graphs provide visual tools for understanding motion and extracting quantitative information.
common_misconceptions: The slope of a distance-time graph is acceleration (it is velocity).
The area under a velocity-time graph is distance (it is displacement).
Curved graphs always mean acceleration (depends on the graph type).
learning_objectives: Plot and interpret distance-time graphs.
Plot and interpret velocity-time graphs.
Calculate speed/velocity from the slope of a distance-time graph.
Calculate acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph.
Calculate displacement from the area under a velocity-time graph.

entities.name: Gravitation
entities.definition: The natural phenomenon by which all objects with mass or energy are attracted toward one another. Gravitation is a fundamental interaction that governs the motion of planets, stars, galaxies, and the structure of the universe.
common_misconceptions: Gravity only exists on Earth (gravitation is universal — it acts between all masses).
Gravity requires air to act (gravitation acts through vacuum).
Lighter objects experience no gravity (all masses experience gravitational attraction).
learning_objectives: Describe gravitation as a universal attractive force between masses.
Explain why objects fall toward Earth.
Distinguish between gravitation and gravity (gravity is Earth's gravitational pull).
real_world_applications: Tides (Moon's gravitational pull on Earth's oceans).

entities.name: Gravitational Acceleration
entities.definition: The acceleration experienced by an object solely under the influence of Earth's gravity, near the Earth's surface. It is approximately constant for all objects, regardless of their mass.
common_misconceptions: g is the same everywhere in the universe (g varies with distance from a massive body).
g is a force (g is an acceleration; the force is weight = m·g).
Heavier objects have larger g (g is independent of the falling object's mass).
learning_objectives: State the approximate value of g near Earth's surface.
Distinguish between gravitational acceleration and gravitational force.
Apply g in free-fall and projectile motion calculations.
real_world_applications: Parachuting (terminal velocity involves balancing g with air resistance).

entities.name: Heat
entities.definition: Energy transferred from one body to another due to a temperature difference. Heat is energy in transit — it is not stored in an object (the stored energy is internal energy).
entities.equation: Q = m·c·ΔT (specific heat) ; Q = m·L (latent heat)
common_misconceptions: Heat and temperature are the same (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
Heat is stored in an object (heat is energy in transit; internal energy is stored).
Cold is a form of energy (cold is the absence of heat; heat flows from hot to cold).
learning_objectives: Define heat as energy transfer due to temperature difference.
Distinguish between heat and temperature.
Calculate heat transfer using specific heat capacity.
Explain why objects reach thermal equilibrium.
real_world_applications: Climate and weather (heat transfer in atmosphere).
key_experiments: Measuring specific heat capacity of a metal using calorimetry.
Observing heat transfer between hot and cold water.

entities.name: Heating Effect of Electric Current
entities.definition: The phenomenon by which electrical energy is converted to thermal energy when current flows through a conductor with resistance. The heat produced depends on the current, resistance, and time.
common_misconceptions: All electrical energy becomes heat (some becomes light, mechanical energy, etc.).
Heating effect is always undesirable (it's useful in heaters, fuses, and bulbs).
Thicker wires heat more (thicker wires have less resistance and heat less).
learning_objectives: Explain the heating effect of electric current.
Calculate heat produced using H = I²Rt.
Describe applications: electric heaters, fuses, bulbs.
Explain why wires heat up when current flows.

entities.name: Impulse
entities.definition: The product of the average force acting on an object and the time interval over which it acts. Impulse equals the change in momentum of the object.
entities.unit: newton second (N·s) or kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s)
common_misconceptions: Impulse is the same as force (impulse is force × time; it measures total momentum change).
A small force cannot produce significant impulse (over a long enough time, even small forces produce large impulse).
Impulse only occurs in collisions (any force acting over time produces impulse).
learning_objectives: Define impulse as force multiplied by time.
Relate impulse to change in momentum.
Explain how increasing collision time reduces average force.
Interpret force-time graphs to find impulse.
real_world_applications: Catching a ball (pulling hand back increases time, reduces force).
Pole vaulters landing on thick mats.

entities.name: Inertia
entities.definition: The tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of motion — whether at rest or moving with constant velocity. Inertia is not a force; it is a property of matter quantified by mass.
common_misconceptions: Inertia is a force that pushes objects forward (inertia is resistance to change, not a force).
Heavier objects have more inertia because gravity pulls harder on them (inertia is mass, not weight).
Inertia only applies to objects at rest (it applies equally to objects in motion).
learning_objectives: Define inertia as resistance to change in motion.
Relate inertia to mass — greater mass means greater inertia.
Explain everyday phenomena using inertia.
real_world_applications: Shaking a tree branch to dislodge fruit.

entities.name: Kinetic Energy
entities.definition: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion. The kinetic energy of an object depends on its mass and the square of its speed.
common_misconceptions: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed (it depends on speed squared — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy).
Kinetic energy can be negative (kinetic energy is always non-negative).
Heavier objects always have more kinetic energy (at the same speed, yes; at different speeds, not necessarily).
learning_objectives: Define kinetic energy as energy of motion.
Calculate kinetic energy from mass and speed.
Explain why kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Relate kinetic energy to work done on an object.
real_world_applications: Vehicle braking distance (doubles with the square of speed).
Sports (a faster ball has much more energy).
Wind turbines (kinetic energy of wind converted to electricity).

entities.name: Lens
entities.definition: A transparent optical device that refracts light to converge or diverge rays. Convex (converging) lenses bring light to a focus; concave (diverging) lenses spread light apart.
common_misconceptions: All lenses magnify (concave lenses reduce image size).
Lenses work by reflection (they work by refraction).
Thicker lenses always have shorter focal length (depends on curvature and refractive index).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between convex and concave lenses.
Draw ray diagrams for image formation by lenses.
Use the lens formula to calculate image position.
Explain how lenses are used in optical instruments.
key_experiments: Finding the focal length of a convex lens.
Drawing ray diagrams for different object positions.

entities.name: Light
entities.definition: Electromagnetic radiation that is visible to the human eye. Light behaves both as a wave and as a particle (photon), though at Grade 10 the wave model predominates.
entities.equation: c = f·λ (c = speed of light in vacuum ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s)
common_misconceptions: Light needs a medium to travel (light travels through vacuum).
Light travels instantaneously (it has finite speed).
Light is only what we can see (visible light is a small part of the EM spectrum).
learning_objectives: Describe light as a form of electromagnetic radiation.
State the speed of light in vacuum.
Explain that light can travel through vacuum.
Distinguish between luminous and non-luminous objects.

entities.name: Magnetic Field
entities.definition: The region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where magnetic forces can be detected. Magnetic fields are represented by field lines that show the direction and strength of the field.
common_misconceptions: Magnetic field lines are real physical objects (they are a model to represent the field).
Magnetic fields only exist around magnets (current-carrying wires also produce them).
Magnetic field lines cross each other (they never cross).
learning_objectives: Describe the magnetic field as a field of force.
Plot magnetic field lines around bar magnets and current-carrying wires.
Use the right-hand rule to determine field direction.
Explain how magnetic field strength varies with distance.

entities.name: Magnetic Flux
entities.definition: A measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area, calculated as the product of magnetic field strength perpendicular to the surface and the surface area.
common_misconceptions: Magnetic flux and magnetic field strength are identical (flux accounts for total area and orientation).
A stationary coil in a constant magnetic field has changing flux (flux only changes when field, area, or angle changes).
learning_objectives: Define magnetic flux and calculate its value for a surface perpendicular to a uniform field.
State the SI unit of magnetic flux (weber).
Relate rate of change of magnetic flux to induced electromotive force.
real_world_applications: Electric power transformers and induction cooktops.
Magnetic field sensors and hall-effect probes.

provenance.source: IUPAP Symbols, Units, Nomenclature in Physics

entities.name: Magnetism
entities.definition: The phenomenon by which materials exert attractive or repulsive forces on other materials. Magnetism is intimately connected to electricity — moving charges produce magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields produce electric currents.
common_misconceptions: All metals are magnetic (only iron, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys are ferromagnetic).
Magnets attract all metals (only magnetic materials).
Magnetic poles can exist independently (breaking a magnet produces two smaller magnets, each with both poles).
learning_objectives: Describe magnetic materials and their properties.
Identify magnetic poles and their interactions.
Map magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
Distinguish between permanent magnets and electromagnets.

entities.name: Mass
entities.definition: A property of a body that quantifies its resistance to acceleration in Newtonian mechanics; an intrinsic property independent of location.
common_misconceptions: Mass and weight are the same thing (weight is a force, W = m·g, and varies with gravity).

entities.name: Measurement
entities.definition: The process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known standard (unit) to obtain a numerical value. Measurement connects physical quantities to mathematics, enabling quantitative description and prediction.
common_misconceptions: Measurement gives the exact true value of a quantity (all measurements have some uncertainty).
Only laboratory instruments count as measurement (any comparison against a standard is measurement).
learning_objectives: Explain the need for measurement in physics.
Identify sources of measurement error.
Distinguish between precision and accuracy.
key_experiments: Measuring the same object multiple times and observing variation in results.

entities.name: Mechanical Advantage
entities.definition: The factor by which a machine multiplies the input force. Mechanical advantage allows a smaller force to produce a larger force, though over a shorter distance.
common_misconceptions: Machines create energy (they only transform force and distance).
Greater mechanical advantage always means easier work (it means less force over more distance).
Mechanical advantage can be greater than 100% efficient (efficiency is always less than 100%).
learning_objectives: Define mechanical advantage.
Calculate mechanical advantage for simple machines.
Explain the force-distance trade-off.
Calculate efficiency of machines.

entities.name: Mirror
entities.definition: A surface that reflects light. Plane mirrors produce virtual images of the same size; curved (concave and convex) mirrors can produce real or virtual images of varying sizes.
common_misconceptions: All mirrors produce the same type of image (image type depends on mirror shape and object position).
Curved mirrors always magnify (depends on object position).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between plane, concave, and convex mirrors.
Draw ray diagrams for image formation in curved mirrors.
Use the mirror formula to calculate image position.
Explain uses of different types of mirrors.

entities.name: Momentum
entities.definition: The product of a body's mass and velocity; a vector quantity that is conserved in closed systems. Momentum quantifies the "amount of motion" an object possesses.
common_misconceptions: Momentum and kinetic energy are the same kind of quantity (momentum is a vector measured in kg·m/s; kinetic energy is a scalar measured in joules).
A heavier object always has more momentum (momentum depends on both mass and velocity).
Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions (it is conserved in all isolated systems).
learning_objectives: Define momentum as a vector quantity.
Calculate momentum from mass and velocity.
Explain why momentum is a useful quantity in collisions.
Apply the principle of conservation of momentum.
real_world_applications: Car crashes (crumple zones increase collision time, reducing force).
key_experiments: Colliding trolleys on a frictionless track to demonstrate momentum conservation.

entities.name: Motion
entities.definition: The change in position of an object with respect to time and a reference point. Motion is the most fundamental phenomenon studied in mechanics.
common_misconceptions: An object at rest is not in motion relative to anything (motion is relative — it depends on the reference frame).
Motion requires a continuous force (Newton's first law: motion continues without net force).
All motion is along straight lines (motion can be curved or circular).
learning_objectives: Define motion as change in position over time.
Distinguish between different types of motion (linear, circular, periodic).
Use reference points to describe motion.
Classify motion as uniform or non-uniform.

entities.name: Newton's First Law of Motion
entities.definition: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues in motion with constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line), unless acted upon by a net external force.
common_misconceptions: An object in motion naturally comes to rest (friction is the external force stopping it).
No motion means no forces (forces can balance to zero net force).
A constant force is needed to maintain constant velocity (no net force is needed for constant velocity).
learning_objectives: State Newton's first law in words and mathematically.
Explain inertia as the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion.
Analyze situations where balanced forces produce no acceleration.
Recognize that constant velocity implies zero net force.
real_world_applications: Seatbelts (passengers continue forward when a car stops suddenly).
Tablecloth trick (objects at rest tend to stay at rest).
Spacecraft coasting in deep space with engines off.
key_experiments: Air track experiments showing nearly frictionless motion at constant velocity.
Rolling a ball on increasingly smooth surfaces.

entities.name: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
entities.definition: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.
common_misconceptions: Gravity only exists on Earth (gravitation is universal).
Gravity requires air to act (gravitation acts through vacuum).
Heavier objects fall faster (in vacuum, all fall at the same rate).
learning_objectives: State Newton's law of universal gravitation.
Calculate gravitational force between two masses.
Explain why weight varies with location.
Relate gravitation to weight and free fall.

entities.name: Newton's Second Law
entities.definition: The net force acting on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum; at constant mass this reduces to F = m·a.
entities.equation: F = dp/dt (general); F = m·a at constant mass
common_misconceptions: F = m·a means the force is a property of the object itself (F is the net external force acting on the object).

entities.name: Newton's Third Law of Motion
entities.definition: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction on object A.
common_misconceptions: Action and reaction forces cancel each other (they act on different objects, so they cannot cancel).
The stronger object exerts a larger force (forces in an action-reaction pair are always equal).
Action and reaction occur at different times (they are simultaneous).
learning_objectives: State Newton's third law in words and mathematically.
Identify action-reaction force pairs in physical situations.
Explain why action-reaction pairs do not cancel.
Analyze forces on multiple interacting objects.
real_world_applications: Rocket propulsion (exhaust gases push backward; rocket moves forward).
Walking (foot pushes backward on ground; ground pushes forward on foot).
Swimming (water pushed backward; swimmer moves forward).
key_experiments: Two spring balances pulling each other show equal readings.
